difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → cost reduction → improved outcomes). The weakener attacks the move from cost reduction to improved outcomes rather than the policy's cost effects directly. One distractor strengthens; one is out-of-scope.
stimulus: A county health administrator argued that switching from fee-for-service reimbursement to a bundled-payment model reduced hospital spending by 12 percent over two years. She concluded that the bundled-payment model therefore improved patient health outcomes, since lower costs mean fewer unnecessary procedures and less risk of hospital-acquired infections.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the administrator's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several hospitals in neighboring counties adopted bundled payments at the same time and reported similar reductions in spending.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reduction in spending under bundled payments was achieved primarily by discharging patients earlier, before their recoveries were fully confirmed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hospital-acquired infection rates have declined nationally over the past decade regardless of reimbursement model.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bundled-payment models require hospitals to coordinate care across multiple providers, which can increase administrative complexity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Under fee-for-service reimbursement, physicians tend to order more diagnostic tests than under bundled payments.

explanations.correct: The administrator assumes that reduced spending signals fewer unnecessary procedures, which would improve outcomes. Answer B shows the spending reduction came from early discharges — a mechanism that could harm rather than help patient health, severing the assumed link between lower costs and better outcomes.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope: shows the trend is widespread but does nothing to challenge whether lower costs translate to better outcomes in this county.
explanations.B: Correct. Reveals an alternative explanation for the cost reduction that undermines, rather than supports, improved patient outcomes.
explanations.C: Too narrow / irrelevant: addresses only infection rates nationally and doesn't explain whether this county's outcomes improved due to the payment model.
explanations.D: Attacking a peripheral premise: administrative complexity is a cost, not evidence that patient outcomes failed to improve.
explanations.E: Opposite (strengthener): confirms that fee-for-service incentivizes unnecessary tests, which supports the administrator's premise that bundled payments reduce unnecessary procedures.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument with a two-step inference: reduced greenhouse emissions → slowed warming → preserved Arctic habitat. Weakener attacks the second link. Distractors include a strengthener and a subject-shift trap.
stimulus: Environmental researchers at a Nordic institute reported that a newly proposed international agreement would reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by 18 percent within a decade. The researchers concluded that the agreement, if ratified, would prevent the further collapse of Arctic sea-ice habitat critical to polar bear survival.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The proposed agreement has already received preliminary endorsements from the ten largest greenhouse-gas-emitting nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polar bears have demonstrated some ability to adapt their hunting behaviors when sea-ice coverage decreases temporarily.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Arctic sea ice is currently losing volume at a rate driven primarily by ocean heat absorption that has already been locked in by past emissions, meaning an 18 percent future reduction would not meaningfully slow ice loss for several decades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several Arctic species other than polar bears depend on sea-ice habitat for breeding and foraging.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some member nations have historically failed to meet their targets under prior international environmental agreements.

explanations.correct: The researchers' conclusion depends on reduced future emissions translating into preserved Arctic sea ice within a meaningful timeframe. Answer C breaks that link by establishing that sea-ice loss is driven by already-locked-in ocean heat, so the emissions reduction would not prevent further collapse for decades — directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Strengthens the argument by suggesting ratification is likely, making the researchers' conditional conclusion more relevant.
explanations.B: Shift in subject: addresses polar bear behavioral adaptation, not whether sea-ice habitat is preserved — a distractor that doesn't touch the causal chain.
explanations.C: Correct. Attacks the premise that reducing future emissions will halt imminent sea-ice collapse.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: broadens concern to other species but does not weaken the claim about polar bear habitat.
explanations.E: Too narrow: raises doubt about whether the agreement will be honored, but the researchers' conclusion is conditional ('if ratified'), so compliance history is a peripheral issue.

difficultyReason: Analogical argument comparing two technologies. Weakener introduces a disanalogy that breaks the comparison. Distractors include an accurate-but-irrelevant fact and an opposite answer.
stimulus: A technology journalist argued that because voice-recognition software improved dramatically once developers began training it on data sets ten times larger than those previously used, image-recognition software will similarly achieve dramatic improvements if developers simply scale up their training data sets by the same factor.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the journalist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The leading image-recognition software already outperforms human accuracy on several standardized visual classification benchmarks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Voice-recognition software and image-recognition software are both forms of machine-learning applications that rely on large training data sets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Image-recognition software, unlike voice-recognition software, has reached a performance plateau where errors stem primarily from ambiguities in the images themselves rather than from insufficient training data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scaling up training data sets is generally more expensive for image data than for audio data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several major technology companies have announced plans to double their image-recognition training data sets within the next two years.

explanations.correct: The journalist's analogy assumes image-recognition software would respond to more data the way voice-recognition software did. Answer C breaks that analogy by identifying a key disanalogy: image recognition's errors are not data-quantity problems, so adding more data would not produce the same gains.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope: current performance level doesn't address whether more data would cause further improvement.
explanations.B: Strengthens the analogy by confirming the two technologies share relevant structural features.
explanations.C: Correct. Introduces a disanalogy that undermines the journalist's analogical reasoning.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant: addresses cost, not whether the improvement would occur — a classic 'accurate but irrelevant' trap.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope: describes plans to scale data but doesn't speak to whether doing so will produce dramatic improvement.

difficultyReason: Causal argument from correlation in an economics context. Weakener provides an alternative explanation for the observed correlation. One distractor attacks a premise without touching the conclusion; one strengthens.
stimulus: A financial analyst observed that in the twelve months following each of the last four recessions, companies that increased their advertising budgets grew their market share by an average of 9 percent, while companies that cut advertising budgets lost an average of 6 percent. The analyst concluded that increased advertising spending is what caused the market-share gains during post-recession recoveries.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Companies that increased advertising budgets during post-recession periods also tended to have stronger underlying balance sheets, which independently enabled them to pursue growth strategies unavailable to struggling competitors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The four recessions examined by the analyst varied considerably in duration and in the industries they affected most severely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Advertising costs tend to fall during recessions, making it cheaper for financially healthy companies to increase their advertising spending.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some companies that maintained flat advertising budgets during the post-recession periods also experienced modest market-share growth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Market-share gains are one of the most reliable indicators of long-term revenue growth for consumer-goods companies.

explanations.correct: The analyst infers causation from correlation. Answer A provides an alternative explanation — stronger balance sheets, not advertising itself, drove growth — because financially healthier companies could pursue multiple growth strategies simultaneously. This severs the causal link the analyst asserts.
explanations.A: Correct. Classic alternative-explanation weakener: a third variable (financial health) explains both the ability to increase advertising and the ability to gain market share.
explanations.B: Attacking a peripheral premise: variation across recessions raises a methodological concern about sample consistency but doesn't offer an alternative cause for the observed gains.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant to causation: lower advertising costs explains why spending increased but not whether that spending caused the gains.
explanations.D: Too narrow: flat-budget companies' modest gains are consistent with the analyst's conclusion and arguably weaken it only weakly; it doesn't provide a better causal account.
explanations.E: Shift in subject: relevance of market share to revenue is a separate claim and does nothing to challenge the advertising-causation inference.

difficultyReason: Predictive policy argument where the weakener attacks the assumption that the predicted mechanism will operate in this context. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope fact.
stimulus: A city council member proposed mandatory minimum sentencing for repeat vandalism offenses, arguing that because mandatory minimums for repeat drunk driving reduced such incidents in three comparable cities by 30 percent over five years, the same policy applied to vandalism will produce a comparable reduction in vandalism rates in this city.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the council member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vandalism is most frequently committed by juveniles, who are typically exempt from mandatory minimum sentencing statutes, whereas repeat drunk driving is predominantly an adult offense.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The three cities that adopted mandatory minimums for drunk driving also increased funding for public transportation during the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing is opposed by several civil liberties organizations on constitutional grounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vandalism rates in this city have increased by 15 percent over the past two years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat offenders in other categories of property crime have been effectively deterred by mandatory minimum sentences in jurisdictions that have implemented them.

explanations.correct: The council member analogizes drunk-driving mandatory minimums to vandalism. Answer A breaks the analogy by identifying a critical disanalogy: the primary vandalism offenders (juveniles) are exempt from mandatory minimums, so the policy's deterrent mechanism cannot reach the offenders it needs to deter.
explanations.A: Correct. Disanalogy trap: the key population committing vandalism is not subject to the policy, so the analogized mechanism fails.
explanations.B: Too narrow: raises an alternative explanation for the drunk-driving reduction (confound), which weakens confidence in the analogy's basis but is less direct than A in attacking whether the policy will work for vandalism here.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope: constitutional opposition speaks to political feasibility, not to whether the policy would reduce vandalism rates if enacted.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant: establishing baseline trend doesn't address whether mandatory minimums will reduce vandalism going forward.
explanations.E: Strengthens: extending the pattern of deterrence to other property crimes supports the analogy the council member is drawing.

difficultyReason: Medical causal argument where the weakener provides an alternative explanation for observed improvements. One distractor is an opposite answer; one is a subject-shift trap.
stimulus: Researchers at a university medical center reported that patients who received acupuncture treatments twice weekly for eight weeks showed a statistically significant reduction in self-reported chronic lower-back pain. The researchers concluded that acupuncture directly reduces chronic lower-back pain.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients who received sham acupuncture — in which needles were placed at clinically irrelevant points — reported pain reductions nearly identical to those reported by patients receiving genuine acupuncture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some patients who completed the eight-week acupuncture regimen reported that their pain returned to prior levels within three months of stopping treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic lower-back pain is among the most common reasons adults in industrialized nations seek medical treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several patients who received acupuncture also independently began low-impact exercise routines during the eight-week study period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acupuncture has been used as a therapeutic practice in parts of East Asia for more than two thousand years.

explanations.correct: If sham acupuncture produces the same reduction in pain, the improvement cannot be attributed to the specific mechanism of genuine acupuncture. Answer A suggests placebo effect or therapeutic attention — not the acupuncture itself — caused the pain reduction, directly undermining the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Sham-control comparison reveals that the active ingredient in acupuncture is not responsible for the improvement, implicating placebo or non-specific effects.
explanations.B: Too narrow: addresses durability of effects, not whether acupuncture directly caused the initial reduction — a different claim than the one being evaluated.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope: prevalence of the condition is irrelevant to whether acupuncture causally reduces it.
explanations.D: Alternative explanation (confound): this also weakens the conclusion, but answer A is a more direct and controlled counterexample, making A the stronger weakener.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant: historical usage does not establish or undermine a causal claim about the mechanism of pain reduction.

difficultyReason: Causal-predictive argument in linguistics. The weakener attacks the inference from a historical pattern to a future outcome by identifying a relevant dissimilarity. Distractors include a strengthener and an accurate-but-irrelevant choice.
stimulus: A linguist argued that when a minority language community's children begin attending schools conducted entirely in the dominant national language, the minority language typically becomes extinct within three generations. She therefore predicted that the Veltari language, spoken by a small community whose children recently began attending exclusively national-language schools, will become extinct within three generations.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studies of language extinction consistently show that economic pressure to assimilate accelerates the shift away from minority languages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Veltari community has established a network of after-school language immersion programs and has made Veltari literacy a condition for participation in community cultural events, practices not present in communities where extinction followed school-language shifts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Veltari has no official written orthography, which makes formal instruction in the language more difficult.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The national language in the Veltari community's country is spoken by more than forty million people.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Language extinction has been documented in communities that never shifted their school instruction to a dominant language.

explanations.correct: The linguist generalizes from past cases of language extinction following school-language shifts. Answer B identifies features of the Veltari community — immersion programs and cultural incentives for language use — that were absent in those historical cases, breaking the analogy and reducing confidence that the same outcome will follow.
explanations.A: Strengthens: confirms a factor (economic pressure) that likely operates in many language-shift contexts, supporting the extinction prediction.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces a disanalogy between the Veltari community and the communities from which the extinction pattern was derived.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant trap: lack of a written orthography might hinder formal instruction, but this detail doesn't bear on whether the historical extinction pattern applies here — it could support the prediction as easily as undermine it.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: the dominant language's speaker population is irrelevant to whether the Veltari-specific pattern will follow historical precedent.
explanations.E: Shift in subject: establishes that school-language shift is not necessary for extinction, not that it won't cause extinction here.

difficultyReason: Ethical-economics argument where a conclusion overreaches from an observed trend to a normative recommendation. The weakener shows that the key premise rests on an incomplete comparison. One distractor strengthens; one attacks a side premise.
stimulus: An economic ethicist argued that companies paying workers the minimum wage are exploiting those workers, because studies consistently show that workers paid at the minimum wage report lower well-being than workers paid above it. He concluded that all companies should be legally required to pay wages above the statutory minimum.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Well-being among minimum-wage workers is also strongly correlated with factors such as job security, workplace relationships, and commute time, which are independent of wage level.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In jurisdictions that have raised the minimum wage significantly, employment rates in low-wage sectors have subsequently declined.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Workers paid above the minimum wage report higher well-being than minimum-wage workers even after controlling for industry type and hours worked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The statutory minimum wage varies considerably across jurisdictions, making a universal mandate difficult to define.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many small businesses operate on margins so thin that raising wages above the minimum would require reducing their workforce.

explanations.correct: The ethicist concludes that minimum-wage pay causes lower well-being and thus constitutes exploitation. Answer A provides an alternative explanation for the lower well-being — independent factors like job security and commute — that severs the causal link between minimum-wage pay specifically and reduced well-being, undermining the exploitation inference.
explanations.A: Correct. Alternative-explanation weakener: the correlation between minimum-wage pay and lower well-being may be driven by confounding variables, not by the wage level itself.
explanations.B: Attacking a side consideration: this is an economic consequence of raising minimums, but the ethicist's argument is about whether current minimum-wage payment is exploitative, not about the effects of raising the minimum.
explanations.C: Strengthens: the controlled comparison bolsters the claim that wage level, not just associated factors, accounts for the well-being difference.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: definitional complexity of a universal mandate is a practical concern, not a challenge to the ethical argument about whether current minimum-wage payment is exploitative.
explanations.E: Shift in subject: small-business costs address the feasibility or economic consequences of a mandate, not whether minimum-wage payment is exploitative.

difficultyReason: Historical causal argument. The weakener offers a confounding event that provides an alternative cause for the observed historical outcome. One distractor is an opposite (strengthener); one is a reversed-causation trap.
stimulus: A historian argued that the introduction of the printing press to Western Europe in the mid-fifteenth century was the primary cause of the rapid spread of the Protestant Reformation in the early sixteenth century, because the Reformation's theological pamphlets reached mass audiences only after the printing press made their wide distribution feasible.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Literacy rates in Western Europe had been rising steadily for more than a century before the printing press was introduced, expanding the potential audience for written theological arguments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The printing press was also used extensively to distribute Catholic counter-Reformation literature, yet Catholicism did not experience a comparable fragmentation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Earlier reform movements in Western Europe, such as those of Jan Hus and John Wycliffe, failed to achieve lasting mass followings despite having theological arguments comparable in content to Luther's.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Protestant Reformation spread most rapidly in regions where pre-existing grievances against the institutional Church were strongest, suggesting those grievances — not print distribution — were the primary driver.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Martin Luther himself credited the printing press as an essential tool in spreading his theological critiques.

explanations.correct: The historian claims the printing press was the primary cause. Answer D offers an alternative primary cause — pre-existing anti-Church grievances — whose geographic pattern better explains where the Reformation spread most rapidly. This directly challenges the printing-press-as-primary-cause conclusion.
explanations.A: Too narrow: rising literacy supports the printing press's eventual impact but doesn't identify an alternative primary cause for the Reformation's spread.
explanations.B: Shift in subject: Catholic fragmentation vs. Protestant fragmentation are different phenomena; the fact that Catholicism didn't fragment despite print access doesn't explain what caused the Reformation to spread.
explanations.C: Strengthens, arguably: the failure of pre-printing-press reform movements supports the historian's argument that the printing press was a decisive new factor.
explanations.D: Correct. Alternative-explanation weakener providing a rival primary cause whose geographic distribution aligns better with where the Reformation took hold.
explanations.E: Opposite (strengthener): Luther's own attribution supports the historian's causal claim.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument from arts/economics context. Weakener attacks the assumption that past patterns will hold under changed conditions. Distractors include a strengthener and an accurate-but-irrelevant choice.
stimulus: A museum director argued that because the museum's last three major traveling exhibitions each increased annual membership enrollment by at least 20 percent, the museum's upcoming traveling exhibition of twentieth-century graphic design will similarly produce at least a 20 percent increase in membership enrollment.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the museum director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Graphic design is a field that has attracted significant popular interest in recent years, and the exhibition will include pieces by several internationally recognized designers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The museum's annual membership enrollment is currently near its historical peak, leaving little room for the 20 percent growth that prior exhibitions achieved from lower baseline enrollment figures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The previous three traveling exhibitions required substantially higher organizational costs than the upcoming graphic design exhibition is projected to require.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Traveling exhibitions are generally more effective at attracting new museum members than permanent collection expansions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The museum's marketing budget for the upcoming exhibition is comparable to the budgets allocated to the previous three successful exhibitions.

explanations.correct: The director assumes that the pattern of 20 percent enrollment growth will repeat. Answer B attacks that assumption by revealing a changed condition — enrollment is near its historical peak — meaning the same absolute growth is arithmetically harder to achieve and prior growth rates are not a reliable baseline for predicting future rates.
explanations.A: Strengthens: popular interest in graphic design and notable designers make it more plausible that the exhibition will attract new members.
explanations.B: Correct. Identifies a changed condition (ceiling effect on enrollment) that makes the historical pattern an unreliable predictor for this case.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant: lower exhibition costs affect profitability, not whether the exhibition will generate membership growth.
explanations.D: Strengthens: confirms traveling exhibitions as a membership-growth driver, supporting the director's prediction.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope: comparable marketing budgets are consistent with similar outcomes but don't address the ceiling-effect problem identified in B, and don't themselves weaken the argument.
